# Plasma cells and plasmacytoid features in thyroid lesions
## Abstract
Rendering the correct diagnosis may be difficult due to the rarity of these lesions, overlapping cytomorphologic features, and challenges selecting the appropriate ancillary studies. This review discusses those thyroid entities showing plasmacytoid cell features and emphasizes their relevance to the recent Bethesda system for reporting thyroid cytopathology and WHO classification of endocrine tumors.
## Illustrative case
These plasma cells were positive for LCA, MUM1, CD138, and kappa light chain, whilst negative for AE1/AE3, CAM 5.2, calcitonin, CEAm, thyroglobulin, HMB45, S100, and CD68. The diagnosis was primary plasmacytoma of the thyroid.
## Introduction
Most thyroid lesions are of epithelial origin and are characterized by a papillary and/or follicular growth architecture. Only a minority show unusual growth patterns [1, 2], such as a predominant solid or spindle cell component, or plasmacytoid, as well as a peculiar biphasic pattern [1, 12].
The detection of a discohesive pattern of predominantly plasmacytoid cells poses a diagnostic challenge, as these cells mimic plasma cells and the differential diagnoses includes benign and malignant primary or metastatic lesions [1, 12]. This review article discusses thyroid entities with a plasmacytoid pattern and offers tips on how to approach these cytological samples.
## Conclusion
The detection of a neoplasm with plasma cells or plasmacytoid appearing cells in a thyroid gland cytology specimen raises a broad differential diagnosis including benign and malignant entities. The presence of these cells in a thyroid sample might represent a common or uncommon lesion.

### Introduction/Objective

Most low-grade B-cell lymphomas of the thyroid are extranodal marginal cell lymphomas (MZL) and may exhibit focal plasma cell differentiation (PCD). PCD could occasionally be extensive, mimicking a true plasma cell neoplasm (PCN). PCN of the thyroid are extremely rare, representing either a component of plasma cell myeloma (PCM), or a primary thyroid extraosseous plasmacytoma (EOPC). We present a case of primary thyroid plasma cell (PC)-rich neoplasm with considerable diagnostic challenge.

### Methods

A 46-year-old male underwent total thyroidectomy for hypothyroidism and compressive symptoms. Microscopically, sheets and nodules of PC with focal plasmablastic features were demonstrated in a background of fibrosing chronic thyroiditis. One benign perithyroidal lymph node was seen. The differential diagnosis included B-cell neoplasm with extensive PCD (ie, MZL or lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma) and PCN.

However, polysomy 18 (seen in 15–33% of B-cell lymphomas, including MZL) was detected. Serum proteins and PCM workup were negative.

The findings were consistent with primary thyroid Kappa-restricted PC-rich neoplasm. While the absence of detectable B-cell neoplastic component was suggestive of EOPC, the diagnosis of MZL with extensive PCD was favored due to the thyroid involvement in a background of thyroiditis, absence of lymph node involvement, detection of polysomy 18, and absence of MYD-88. ### Introduction/Objective

Most low-grade B-cell lymphomas of the thyroid are extranodal marginal cell lymphomas (MZL) and may exhibit focal plasma cell differentiation (PCD). PCD could occasionally be extensive, mimicking a true plasma cell neoplasm (PCN). PCN of the thyroid are extremely rare, representing either a component of plasma cell myeloma (PCM), or a primary thyroid extraosseous plasmacytoma (EOPC). We present a case of primary thyroid plasma cell (PC)-rich neoplasm with considerable diagnostic challenge.

### Methods

A 46-year-old male underwent total thyroidectomy for hypothyroidism and compressive symptoms. Microscopically, sheets and nodules of PC with focal plasmablastic features were demonstrated in a background of fibrosing chronic thyroiditis. One benign perithyroidal lymph node was seen. jina.snippet:
## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3266587/)Abstract

Replacing palpating fingers with an ultrasound (US) probe has resulted in an epidemic of thyroid nodules. Despite the high prevalence of thyroid nodules in the general population, thyroid malignancy is rare. Although no imaging modality can accurately predict the nature of every nodule, high-resolution US is the most sensitive, easily available and cost-effective diagnostic test available to detect thyroid nodules, measure their dimensions and identify their structure. The presence of calcifications, irregular spiculated outline, hypoechogenicity in a solid nodule, chaotic intranodular vascularity and an elongated shape are well-known US features of malignancy in thyroid nodules. Cervical lymph node metastasis and extrathyroidal extension of a thyroid nodule are highly specific for malignancy but seen infrequently. Spongiform nodules, purely or predominantly cystic nodules, nodules with well-defined hypoechoic halo and echogenic as well as isoechoic nodules are usually benign. None of the US characteristics have 100% accuracy in detecting or excluding malignancy. Fine-needle biopsy is currently the best triage test for pre-operative evaluation of a thyroid nodule. There is no significant difference in the risk for malignancy between palpable and non-palpable nodules and size is not a reliable indicator for their malignant potential. The best tool for risk stratification for malignancy in thyroid nodules is US and guided biopsy of nodules with suspicious imaging features. This is especially relevant in patients with multinodular goitre.

If you’ve ever opened an ultrasound report and wondered what that sentence actually means, you’re not alone.

TI-RADS is a scoring system used to describe the ultrasound appearance of thyroid nodules. A TR4 nodule is considered “moderately suspicious,” but that does not mean you have thyroid cancer.

“Recommend correlation” also isn’t a diagnosis. It means the imaging finding needs to be considered alongside the rest of the clinical picture. Depending on the nodule’s size and characteristics, the next step may be observation, repeat ultrasound or a fine-needle biopsy.

The important thing: don’t diagnose yourself from the report. Understand what the report is actually saying—and what it recommends doing next.

Quick Answer

A [thyroid](https://acibademinternational.com/diseases/thyroid-disease/)[ultrasound](https://acibademinternational.com/treatments/ultrasound/) uses sound waves to create detailed images of the thyroid gland and any nodules, showing their size, composition, borders, and suspicious features. Radiologists grade nodules with TI-RADS, a point-based system that scores five characteristics and sorts nodules into five risk levels (TR1 through TR5). That level, combined with the nodule's size, determines whether you need a biopsy, follow-up imaging, or nothing at all.

The gel is cold, the room is dim, and the wand at your throat feels oddly ceremonial. Ten minutes, no needles, no radiation. And then a report lands in your patient portal full of words like _hypoechoic_, _punctate echogenic foci_, and a cryptic _TR4_ and a scan that felt trivial suddenly reads like a verdict.

It isn’t one. Most of what a thyroid ultrasound finds is background noise: small, harmless lumps that a majority of adults quietly carry through life without ever knowing. The trouble is that the report doesn’t sound harmless, and the scoring system radiologists use, TI-RADS, was written for other radiologists, not for you.

So let’s translate it. What the machine actually sees, how those five graded features add up to a score, which findings genuinely deserve attention, and where ultrasound’s vision honestly ends.

Think of it as a structural survey, not a chemistry test. A thyroid ultrasound bounces high-frequency sound waves off the tissues of your neck and converts the returning echoes into a live, moving picture. Abstract:
A 54-year-old male patient was referred to us for a mass in the anterior neck. On examination, he had a solitary thyroid nodule in his right lobe, measuring 5 × 5 cm, approximately. A Tc-99m pertechnetate thyroid scan revealed a cold nodule in the lower two-third of the right lobe of the thyroid. FDG PET scan showed intense FDG uptake in the right lobe nodule. Fine needle aspiration cytology suggested Hashimoto thyroiditis. The histopathology revealed a dense lymphoid infiltrate composed of small monomorphous lymphocytes, plasma cells, and occasional eosinophils. ### Radiology of Thyroid Nodules

#### Brief Summary

**Thyroid nodules** are extremely common and are frequently detected incidentally on:

- Ultrasound
- CT
- MRI
- PET/CT
- Carotid imaging.

The principal radiologic goal is not simply to identify a thyroid nodule, but to estimate the risk of malignancy and determine whether:

- No further evaluation is needed
- Ultrasound surveillance is appropriate
- Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) is indicated.

**High-resolution ultrasound is the primary imaging modality** for thyroid nodule characterization.

Important sonographic features include:

- Composition
- Echogenicity
- Shape
- Margins
- Echogenic foci
- Evidence of extrathyroidal extension
- Associated cervical lymphadenopathy.

Risk-stratification systems such as **ACR TI-RADS** integrate these findings to standardize:

- Malignancy risk assessment
- FNA thresholds
- Follow-up recommendations.

Features associated with increased malignancy risk include:

- Solid composition
- Marked hypoechogenicity
- Taller-than-wide shape
- Irregular or infiltrative margins
- Punctate echogenic foci
- Extrathyroidal extension
- Suspicious cervical lymph nodes.

Features strongly favoring benignity include:

- Pure cystic composition
- Spongiform architecture
- Comet-tail artifacts associated with colloid.

CT and MRI are generally not used to characterize routine thyroid nodules but are valuable for:

- Large goiters
- Retrosternal extension
- Local invasion
- Mediastinal disease
- Advanced thyroid malignancy.

---

### 1. Epidemiology

Thyroid nodules are common, particularly with increasing:

- Age
- Female sex
- Use of high-resolution imaging.

Ultrasound can detect nodules in a substantial proportion of otherwise asymptomatic adults.

Most thyroid nodules are:

- Benign.

Only a minority represent:

- Thyroid carcinoma.

Posted by

HealthTree

Last updated and reviewed on: September 10, 2026

For most people, the path toward a thyroid cancer diagnosis starts with a small, unexpected discovery. You might feel a lump while buttoning a collar or fastening a necklace. Your doctor might feel it during a routine physical exam. Or, most commonly of all, a nodule (an abnormal growth of cells that forms a lump within the thyroid gland) might be spotted by accident on a CT scan, MRI, or ultrasound done for a completely different reason, such as a car accident evaluation or a carotid artery check. Thyroid nodules rarely cause pain or other symptoms on their own, so finding one usually depends on someone looking closely at the right place, whether that is your own hand, your doctor's exam, or a radiologist reading a scan.

Once a nodule is found, you are usually not managed by just one doctor.

- Your primary care doctor often makes the first discovery and orders initial blood work.

- From there, care commonly moves to an endocrinologist (a doctor who specializes in hormone-producing glands like the thyroid), who directs the workup and interprets results in context.

- A radiologist reads your ultrasound and any other imaging.

- If a biopsy is needed, either the endocrinologist or a radiologist may perform it, and a pathologist (a doctor who examines cells and tissue under a microscope) reads the sample.

- If surgery becomes necessary, an endocrine surgeon, a surgeon with specific training in thyroid and parathyroid operations, takes over that part of your care.

This team approach is normal and is a sign of careful, thorough evaluation rather than a cause for alarm.

Here is the most important fact to hold onto as you start this process: the large majority of thyroid nodules are not cancer. Research summarized by the American Thyroid Association shows that by age 60, about half of all people have a thyroid nodule that can be found by exam

seltz.title: Thyroid Nodules - How Ultrasound Differentiates Between Benign and Suspicious Nodules
seltz.snippet:
Dr. Segnini

##### **A Common Finding:**

Thyroid nodules are masses or lumps that form within the thyroid gland, located at the base of the neck. They are extremely common (it is estimated that up to 50-65% of the population may have them), and the vast majority (more than 90%) are benign. Ultrasound is the cornerstone for evaluating them, as it allows us to see what palpation cannot and guides crucial clinical decisions.

##### **Why is Ultrasound the Ideal Technique?**

It is the method of choice because:

- It does not use ionizing radiation.

- It is accessible and inexpensive.

- It has high resolution for superficial structures such as the thyroid.

- It evaluates real-time characteristics that are key to risk.

- It accurately guides fine needle aspiration (FNA) biopsies to obtain samples.

##### **Ultrasound Characteristics: The Language of the Image**

The radiologist carefully analyzes each nodule according to a series of visual patterns. This is the essence of the diagnosis:

##### **Characteristics that suggest BENIGNITY:**

1. Simple cyst: Completely anechoic (black in the image), with well-defined edges. Contains only fluid. Almost no risk.

1. Spongiform: “Honeycomb” appearance, with multiple echogenic (white) microspaces. Very typical of hyperplastic nodules.

1. Hyperechoic with complete halo: A dark (hyperechoic) nodule surrounded by a clear, uniform ring, which usually indicates that it is encapsulated.

1. Acoustic shadow macrocalcifications: Large calcifications that cast a dark shadow behind them, often seen in old and degenerated nodules.

#### **Features that suggest HIGH SUSPICION of MALIGNANCY (Cancer):**

1. Solid hypoechogenicity: Being completely solid and darker than the surrounding neck muscle.

1. Irregular or spiculated margin: Poorly defined edges, with extensions into normal thyroid tissue (like “spikes”).

A thyroid nodule is a growth or lump that forms within the thyroid gland. Most thyroid nodules are benign (non-cancerous), but some can be malignant (cancerous). They are often found incidentally during imaging studies like ultrasound.

Thyroid nodules are a common finding, identified by physical examination in about 5% to 7% of adults. Autopsy studies, however, reveal a prevalence as high as 50% for nodules larger than 1 cm in individuals without known thyroid disease. The detection of nodules has increased significantly, largely due to the widespread use of imaging techniques such as ultrasound (US), as well as CT, MRI, and PET scans. While the vast majority—over 90%—are benign and clinically insignificant, thyroid nodules are relevant because approximately 4% to 6.5% may be malignant.

How to evaluate a Thyroid Nodule

The ACR TI-RADS is a standardized ultrasound-based classification system for evaluating thyroid nodules, created by the American College of Radiology. It offers a point-based framework to help determine whether a nodule requires fine needle aspiration (FNA), follow-up imaging, or can be confidently deemed benign and left without further intervention.

## **Classification of goiter**

There are several classifications of goiter depending on etiology, epidemiology, anatomy, as well as functional or morphological features.

### **By etiology and epidemiology**

- **Physiologic enlargement** is due to the body’s increased need for thyroid hormones (puberty, pregnancy, lactation).
- **Pathologic goiter** occurs as a consequence of thyroid disease.
- **Endemic goiter,** revealed in a large population, is caused by iodine deficiency.

  - **Diffuse goiter:** thyroid gland is uniformly enlarged.

Most thyroid nodules are harmless. This is the most important sentence in this blog post, and hence comes first. However, nobody can help feeling worried upon seeing a lump on an imaging report, especially with all that medical jargon. **Thyroid nodule ultrasound** cannot tell with certainty what kind of nodule a person has, but it can distinguish between those which require further investigation and those which don't. This blog explains how to read your **thyroid nodule ultrasound** report, what the score means, and who really needs a needle test.

## What a Thyroid Nodule Ultrasound Actually Shows

The nodules are very common. Many adults have them without realising it, since these are normally found incidentally while scanning for another condition. About 5 to 10 out of every 100 are cancerous, and most are of the slowly growing kind and have a good prognosis.

A **thyroid nodule ultrasound** uses sound waves, so there's no radiation and no fasting. It provides information about the size, consistency (solid or fluid), margins, shape, and small areas of calcium deposition. It also involves scanning the lymph nodes in the neck. The doctors find it more worrying if it is solid and dark as compared to being smooth and fluid-filled. A thyroid-stimulating hormone level is normally tested in blood to check if the nodule is producing additional hormones.

Most reports will have a TI-RADS classification at the end. The classification works by awarding points for any suspicious signs, adding them together to give you a total of 1 to 5, with 5 being the most suspicious. The follicles were lined by enlarged follicular cells without Hürthle cell change and showed prominent infiltration of the follicular epithelium by lymphocytes, resembling lymphoepithelial-like lesions (Fig. 1B). The 4 mm nodule comprised mildly dilated follicles with similar intraepithelial lymphocytosis within background sclerotic stroma, suggestive of a pre-existing adenomatoid nodule that had regressed after treatment.
